passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: The most common AI system in a company today is an assistant that answers business questions from a warehouse. It is also the easiest one to ship wrong, because a wrong number looks exactly like a right one. This is how I built one, measured it before anyone trusted it, hardened it after the measurements, and what I would tell an AI engineer who is about to build the next one. Employer data is left out; the engineering is not. The public counterpart, on data anyone can inspect, is Quaesitor.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: Non-technical staff want answers to questions like how many active customers did we have in Q2 in Germany, and analysts are the bottleneck between them and the warehouse. The assistant lets them ask in their own words and get a number, a chart and the query that produced it. "Working" is not "answers a demo question well". It is: on a fixed set of real questions with verified answers, the share that comes back correct, the share that comes back wrong without saying so, and the share that correctly declines because the data cannot answer. Those three numbers are the product, and every decision below was made to move them.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: The first version I inherited was a ~4 500-line bespoke NL→SQL service: Vanna for retrieval over ChromaDB, a custom pipeline of prompts, and a growing body of Python that encoded what the business meant by its own words. It was replaced by a ~400-line LangGraph agent behind FastAPI on the Anthropic API, with MCP connectors to BigQuery (the warehouse), OpenMetadata (the catalogue and glossary) and Metabase (the certified dashboards). The decisive design choice: domain knowledge lives in the data catalogue, as glossary terms, descriptions and lineage that analysts already maintain, and the agent reads it at run time. Nothing about what a "customer" or a "tier" means is in the codebase. The rebuild was chosen on maintenance cost per line, and it had to be at parity on the golden sets before it replaced anything.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: The graph is deliberately small: understand the question, look the terms up in the catalogue first, find the certified figure if one exists, otherwise write a query, run it read-only, reconcile, answer with provenance. Every step is a node with a typed state, so a run can be replayed from its trace and a change to one node is testable alone. The agent does not get a schema dump in the prompt; it gets tools to look things up, which keeps the context small and makes the catalogue, not the prompt, the thing to fix when it is wrong.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: A number from an LLM is a claim. The protocol turns it into a checked claim or a refusal. Catalogue first: business terms resolve through the glossary before any SQL is written, so "active customer" means what the company decided it means. Cross-check every figure: when a certified dashboard carries the same measure, the assistant's number is reconciled against it and the difference is reported; when none exists, the answer says it is unreconciled. Compliance is a metric: whether a run followed the protocol is scored in the evaluation harness alongside correctness, so a right answer reached the wrong way counts against the system. Trust is not a property of the model. It is a property of the protocol around it, and protocols can be measured.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: The same idea, in public, is the whole of Quaesitor: plant the reasons a number goes wrong in a warehouse, ask questions with known answers three times each, and count. There the silent-failure rate of frontier models ranges from 56 % to 92 % depending on the pack, and a follow-up study shows that nothing visible at run time predicts which answers are the wrong ones, which is why the cross-check is not optional.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: Everything in this section was done because a measurement said so, not because a checklist did. Tool surface: the connectors exposed 40 MCP tools, 18 of them write-capable. An assistant that can drop a table does not need to, so the surface was cut to a 15-tool read-only allowlist, and a project-scoping wrapper rejects any query that reaches outside the user's project before it gets to BigQuery. Least privilege at the wall, not in the prompt: the assistant ran as a service account, which made it a confused deputy, a user could make the assistant's credentials do what the user's own could not. The fix was per-domain protection enforced at BigQuery IAM. A prompt is a suggestion; IAM is a wall. Cost caps: a single unbounded question consumed 4.07 million input tokens and $21 without failing, because nothing said it should. Hard caps on tokens, tool calls and wall time were added the same day, and cost is now a first-class field of every trace.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: Tracing without names: every run writes fourteen fields, including a salted hash of the user, their team, the tools called, tokens in and out, latency, cost and the protocol-compliance flags, and never a name, never a raw tool output. That is an observability decision and a privacy decision at once, and it is why the traces can be kept and analysed. The traces found a defect nobody had reported: a third-party MCP server returned a malformed output schema that silently discarded results, non-deterministically. Without per-run tool logs that would have been "the assistant is sometimes wrong".

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: The golden sets came from the stakeholders, not from me. The first business POC ran with sales leads, a team manager and a category owner in the room: their real questions became date-fixed golden cases with verified answers; every ambiguous definition they argued about, category semantics, tier models, credit balances, was driven to an authoritative answer and written into the OpenMetadata glossary, so the agent inherits it instead of re-deriving it per question. The harness runs the golden sets on every change and reports correctness, silent failure, refusals and protocol compliance; a change that improves one at the expense of another is visible before it ships. Evaluation is not a phase at the end. It is the loop.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: Measure before you trust, and measure silent failure, not accuracy; a model that is confidently wrong 60 % of the time can have a demo that looks perfect. Put knowledge where people already maintain it, in the catalogue, not in the prompt or the code. Treat the agent as a user with least privilege, enforced where it cannot be talked out of. Cap everything that can grow without bound, and log cost per run from day one. Trace every run pseudonymously so the traces can be kept. Get golden questions from the people who will ask them, fix the dates, and run them in CI. And when you cannot see which answers are wrong from the outside, which the data say you cannot, build the cross-check instead of hoping.

passages.title: AI over data, measured.
passages.text: The live demonstration of these rules on this site is Ask the site: an agent over this site's own data files and texts, with every number coming from a tool call, every quotation verified verbatim, a cap per question, a budget per day, and the trace shown to the user. It is small on purpose; the rules are the point.

passages.text: Forty-seven Czech TV spots from thirteen brands, read three ways: what colour the picture actually commits to, whether voice or music carries the sound, and what a language model sees when it reads the homepage instead of the brief. Then a tool that scores any spot URL against its sector, and one prediction I wrote down before the data came in.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: Brand positioning is usually asserted in a deck and never checked against what the brand puts on screen. The series checks. Each piece answers one question with one technique, each has a reproducible pipeline (fetch → extract → measure → render), each publishes its derived metrics, and none redistributes the source material. It was built across a few weekends to see what competitive brand analysis looks like when it starts from public data instead of pitch decks.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: A spot's picture either commits to the brand colour or commits to a world. Sample every spot at one frame per second, take the five dominant colours per frame with K-means in CIE-LAB, find the spot's dominant chromatic hue, and measure the angle on the hue wheel between it and the brand's own anchor swatch. Beyond about 90° the two are, perceptually, different colours.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: Sixteen spots sit under 20°: Lidl, Penny, T-Mobile, Vodafone flood the screen with their colour. Eleven sit over 100°: Albert's five spots at 150–178°, Komerční banka, AAA Auto, Pilsner Urquell, whose brand green occupies 0.2 % of the picture. Twenty sit in between, and that middle is the finding: most Czech spots are not choosing. AAA Auto's brand yellow occupies 0.001 % of screen time; the picture is a used-car catalogue in greys and browns, with a logo on it.

passages.text: fig. 1 · Hue distance between brand anchor and dominant on-screen colour, one bar per spot, sorted. Recomputed for this page from the study's published metrics.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: Is that just sector? Hierarchical clustering on the energy distance between every pair of brands' weighted LAB palettes says no: brands cluster across sector boundaries by their colour signature, not by what they sell. Saturation tension, the spread of saturation across a spot, is a second axis that does split by category, banking and automotive flat, performative formats swinging.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: Same 47 spots, audio only. Voice activity with silero-vad, tempo by beat tracking, key by Krumhansl–Schmuckler correlation, brightness and dynamics with librosa. Voice-led means more than half the runtime is speech. The result is a cliff: 44 spots are voice-led, three are music-led, none is mixed. Pilsner Urquell's Alfons is 86 % music; two McDonald's image spots are 77 % and 76 %; the next spot down is 41 %. There is no music-led promotional spot in the corpus at all.

passages.text: fig. 2 · Voice and music share of runtime, one bar per spot, sorted by music. Three cross the line. Recomputed from the study's metrics.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: The defaults are narrow in every other dimension too: tempo lives in one band (110–140 bpm holds 23 of 47), and the mode skews minor, 27 of 47, even for retail promos. Czech advertising diversifies how it looks and converges on how it sounds. "Music carries the spot" is a normal creative variable elsewhere; here it is essentially unused, which makes it cheap to occupy.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: Scrape the homepages of thirty major Czech brands (title, description, first headings, first paragraphs; 24 succeeded, 6 were behind anti-bot walls or empty, which is reported rather than hidden), embed them with a multilingual sentence model, reduce with UMAP, cluster. Put rising Czech search queries into the same space.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: The map's boundaries do not match the sectors. ČSOB, Česká spořitelna, Fio, Air Bank, Komerční banka, Generali, ČEZ and Škoda Auto land in one neighbourhood: five banks, an insurer, a utility and a carmaker, one institutional register. The words that define that neighbourhood against the other three are banka, škoda, čez, fio, česká. A challenger bank's positioning, "the bank that is different from Komerční", is decided in the campaign layer and quietly undone in the homepage layer. With 54 points UMAP coordinates are approximate topology, not distances; the opportunity scoring is done in the original 768 dimensions, and the page says so.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: Spot Scorer takes the two pipelines and turns them into something a strategist can use on Monday: pick a spot, see its colour and audio metrics against the sector median, and the four or five numerical targets it would have to hit to leave its category default. Paste any YouTube, Facebook or Instagram URL and a Modal backend runs the full pipeline in about 25 seconds.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: Put the two commitments on one plane and the corpus reads itself. Most spots commit on one axis and hedge on the other. Pilsner's Alfons is the one spot that commits to a world by picture (102°, brand green at 0.2 %) and by sound (86 % music, 81 bpm, F♯ major) at once, two pipelines agreeing about one brand. Albert is the opposite: five spots that commit to a world visually (150–178°) and to a voiceover audially (88 % speech). Each decision is extreme on its own axis; the pair does not reinforce. That is the muddle's stealthiest form, decisive metric by metric, conflicted in motion.

passages.text: fig. 3 · The two commitments on one plane. Top right is empty except for Pilsner; Albert commits on the picture and hedges on the sound. Joined from both studies' spot-level metrics.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: On 18 May I wrote down a falsifiable claim before the data could answer it: five spots, three "coherent" (Pilsner, a McDonald's promo, a Lidl brand-colour flood) and two "muddled" (Albert, a Vodafone telecom spot), with the claim that over thirty days the coherent set would gain more YouTube views in total (claim A) and hold the top three ranks (claim B). The confounds were listed in the same file: existing views, subscriber base, paid promotion, the algorithm, all of which matter more than creative coherence, and n = 5. The check was due on 17 June. I forgot it. I ran it while writing this page, 119 days after the baseline.

passages.title: Strategy decks talk about brand. This measures it.
passages.text: Claim A holds on paper, 3 813 against 3 210, and only because of McDonald's, whose spot rides the name of a television show and was flagged as confounded before the fact. Claim B fails: Pilsner, the most coherent spot in the corpus, gained 44 views in four months and finished last. The Lidl spot was taken private, which is its own answer about how long promo creative lives. The methodology measures the spot; YouTube measures the spot plus everything else. The series is descriptive, not predictive of reach, and the file said that too. What I would keep from the exercise is the habit, not the result: write the claim down first, with the ways it could be wrong, and run the check even when it is late.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: A migration is finished when nothing changed. Not "the tests pass", not "the numbers look right": zero mismatches across every column and an identical fingerprint for every day, computed before a single consumer is repointed. I used the method on a five-year salary pipeline and a 62-day event backfill. This is it as a tool anyone can run, and what it found on its first real dataset.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: Two cutovers from the day job. A salary-recompute pipeline moved from a standalone extractor to an incremental dbt-python model; before any downstream consumer was repointed, the new model was compared with the old one across five years of history and twenty columns, and the result was zero mismatches. A production GA4 event-stream backfill was validated by a full-row fingerprint per day: 62 of 62 days identical to the pre-backfill snapshot, development identical to production. Neither argument was "we tested it". Both were a number, and the number was zero.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: The method behind both is small enough to be a package. Two tables, a key, optionally a partition column, and a fixed sequence of questions asked in an order where each one only makes sense if the previous one passed. cutover is that sequence, in DuckDB over Arrow tables, with a text, JSON and self-contained HTML report and exit codes that a CI job can gate on.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: 1 · Schema. Columns only on one side, and shared columns whose type changed. The comparison continues on the shared columns with equal types; the rest is reported, and by default any of it fails the run. A type change is not a formatting detail. It is usually the first symptom of a different pipeline making different assumptions, which the demo below illustrates.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: 2 · Key. NULL keys and duplicate keys on each side. A non-unique key on either side fails with key_not_unique and the column step is skipped, because a per-column diff on a non-unique key would silently compare arbitrary pairs of rows and report nonsense with confidence.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: 3 · Row set. Keys only in the old table, keys only in the new, keys in both. Counts and samples. Most cutover failures are here: a filter that changed, a source that was late, a join that dropped the rows with no match.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: 4 · Columns. On keys present on both sides, per column, the number of rows where the values differ, with NULL = NULL. Exact equality for everything except floats and decimals with a declared tolerance, where two values are the same when

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: Every tolerance is declared per column and printed in the report, so a reader can see what was allowed to differ. A tolerance you did not declare does not exist; the tool does not decide on its own that 12.059999999999999 is 12.06.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: 5 · Fingerprints. For each value of the partition column, a hash of all rows in that partition ordered by key, on each side. The report says identical / total partitions and lists the ones that differ, which is how "62 of 62 days" is computed. The hash is exact, so columns with a declared tolerance are excluded from it and the report says which. If the partition column itself changed type, the fingerprints are not computed at all and the reason is partition_type_differs; comparing the hash of 2025-01-01 with the hash of 2025-01-01 00:00:00 would report 66 partitions for 33 days, which is what the first version of the tool did on the demo before the demo corrected it.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: 6 · Verdict. PASS only when the schema is clean, the key is unique, both row-set differences are zero, every column has zero mismatches within its declared tolerance and every partition fingerprint matches. Anything else is FAIL, with a list of reasons a script can read.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: The sequence matters. Comparing columns before checking the key gives confident nonsense. Comparing fingerprints before comparing columns tells you that a day differs without telling you why. Comparing values before comparing schema hides that a DATE became a TIMESTAMP.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: A month of NYC yellow-taxi trips, January 2025, about 3.3 million rows in one public parquet file. Two independently written aggregations of it into (day, pickup zone) → trips, fare, kilometres: a "legacy" one in pandas, dropping non-positive fares, summing floats, converting miles to kilometres at the end; and a "new" one in SQL in DuckDB with the same intent, rounding the fare sum to cents. Then cutover on the two results with key (day, zone), partition by day, and a 10−6 tolerance on kilometres for the multiplication order.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: Three findings, none of them planted. The type change: DuckDB returned day as a DATE, and the DuckDB-to-pandas bridge turned it into a datetime; the pandas side had a calendar date. Both sides agreed on the key, so a row-count check would have passed. The schema step caught it, and it is the reason the fingerprints refused to run. The 343 fare mismatches: every one of them is floating-point noise, the largest absolute difference is 3.6 × 10−12, the pandas sum of 12.06 arriving as 12.059999999999999 against SQL's rounded 12.06. The tool is right not to forgive it on its own; the fix is a declared half-cent tolerance, visible in the report. The row set: 7 280 groups on both sides, 0 and 0, on 33 days, because the "January" file contains trips dated 31 December and 1 February. That is the source, not the pipelines, and both pipelines agreed on it.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: Both reports are published as the tool wrote them: run 1, run 2, with the JSON next to each. The script that produced them is tools/cutover_demo.py in the site repository; it downloads the file, builds both aggregates, runs both comparisons and writes the reports, so the numbers above come from the run, not from me.

passages.title: How to prove a cutover
passages.text: It does not push the comparison into a remote warehouse; both tables are read into Arrow and compared locally in DuckDB, which spills to disk and is fine for tens of millions of rows and not the right tool for billions. It has no rules for acceptable schema evolution; a rename is a drop and an add. It does not know which side is right. A cutover proof shows that the new thing equals the old thing, and if the old thing was wrong, so is the new one, with a certificate. The judgement about which side to trust stays with the person running it, which is where it belongs.

passages.title: Delayed All the Time. On Time, Occasionally.
passages.text: Five real days of Prague public transport, played as disco tracks by the transport system itself. The metro is the kick drum because it is the most reliable pulse in the city. The buses are the chords, and they go out of tune exactly as far as they run late. When the city stops keeping up, the track lifts into the chorus.

passages.title: Delayed All the Time. On Time, Occasionally.
passages.text: This is the companion piece to a master's thesis on delay persistence in the Prague network, and it started as a way of hearing the thing the thesis was about. Delays are not noise. They are a slowly moving state you can watch; the morning peak builds, holds, and lets go. Statistically it is an autoregression whose coefficients sum to 0.73:

passages.title: Delayed All the Time. On Time, Occasionally.
passages.text: A shock to the delay at one moment is still three-quarters there in the next. Musically it is a build-up, a chorus and a breakdown, and the ear hears it before the table does.

passages.title: Delayed All the Time. On Time, Occasionally.
passages.text: The player is one self-contained HTML file: no server, no build step, no external resources, all audio synthesised live with the Web Audio API from five days of aggregated stop-time data embedded verbatim. No raw records are redistributed; the aggregates are a derived work of Golemio's open data and say so.

passages.title: Delayed All the Time. On Time, Occasionally.
passages.text: Nothing is random. One day is 288 five-minute windows, so one day is 288 beats; at 116 BPM twenty-four hours take about two and a half minutes. Each transport mode is an instrument, and each instrument plays what its mode did in that window.

passages.title: Delayed All the Time. On Time, Occasionally.
passages.text: Song structure is data-driven too. Whenever the smoothed, event-weighted average delay of surface transport (bus, tram, trolleybus) exceeds 68 % of that day's own maximum, the city has stopped keeping up and the track lifts into the chorus. On a typical weekday that yields exactly the two rush hours, roughly 07:25–10:00 and 14:45–17:40, with the delay peaking at 145 s around 07:55. The two beats before each chorus break down into a snare roll and a riser before the drop, because that is what the data does too.

passages.text: fig. 1 · The five days as the record hears them: event-weighted surface delay per 5-minute window, chorus shaded. Recomputed from the player's embedded aggregates for this page; the mean delays match the record's liner notes.

passages.title: Delayed All the Time. On Time, Occasionally.
passages.text: The key is chosen by the day's mean surface delay, from bright modes to dark: under 40 s lydian, under 70 ionian, under 100 dorian, under 130 aeolian, otherwise phrygian.

passages.title: Delayed All the Time. On Time, Occasionally.
passages.text: Production notes, for the record: the groove swings at about 58 % shuffle, everything melodic is side-chained to the metro's kick, the bassline walks chromatically into every chord change, the arrangement varies in eight-beat blocks so long off-peak stretches stay alive, and the mix is stereo (plucks left, arpeggio right, pads wide) with a −4.5 dB high shelf at 6 kHz. Title and structure are a loving homage to the disco-revival tradition. No audio was sampled. Any resemblance to an actual banger is purely statistical.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Everything else on this site is what I do after hours. This is the day job: a cross-cloud data platform for a group of international job portals, the infrastructure that provisions it, the observability that keeps it honest, the access control that keeps it safe, and an LLM assistant over the warehouse that gets measured before it gets trusted. Employer internals are left out; the engineering is not. This page is long on purpose. It is the one page here that is allowed to be an advertisement.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The platform serves several job portals and HR products across AWS and GCP. The seam between the clouds is keyless: AWS Step Functions authenticate to BigQuery through Workload Identity Federation, so there is no service-account key to rotate, leak or forget. The whole stack is infrastructure as code, AWS CDK in Python and Terraform, across production and development accounts: ECS/Fargate services, Lambda, Step Functions, ECR, ALB routing, S3, IAM, Secrets Manager, SSM. Nothing on the platform exists only in a console. If it is not in the repository, it is not there.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Smaller pieces that follow from the same rule. A hand-built Windows bastion, needed to reach a partner MySQL behind an IP allowlist, was captured as IaC: SSM Session Manager only, no inbound security-group rules, no exposed RDP, IMDSv2 required, encrypted root volume. Cross-account backup on RDS and EFS was standardised so backups survive the loss of the source AWS account, arguing against the documented S3 path in favour of versioning and replication. And the dependency chain got the same treatment: shared libraries live in a private AWS CodeArtifact registry as the single source of truth, which is also where the broken wheel metadata that had leaked local paths into published packages was found and fixed.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Two design decisions I would make again. Scoped deployments: the deploy job derives which stacks a change touched from the live CDK construct tree rather than from a hand-maintained lookup table. It is rename-proof, and one broken app no longer blocks the deploy of every other app, which used to be the normal Tuesday. ECR + App stack pairs: eight analytics apps, each one monolithic stack, refactored into an image stack and a runtime stack with shared constructs. The image tag is handed across through SSM Parameter Store instead of CloudFormation exports, so container and runtime configuration deploy independently and an export lock never holds a rollout hostage.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Deploys run from GitHub Actions. The same actions also run the audits described below, on a schedule, so "who checked this" always has the answer "the workflow, at 03:00, here is the log".

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: A dashboard clicked together in the console has three problems: it drifts, it disappears when the account is rebuilt, and nobody reviews it. So dashboards and alarms are CDK constructs that live next to the service they watch, in the same pull request. A new ECS service gets its CloudWatch dashboard and its alarms by construction, and a deleted service takes them with it. The alarms are on service-level objectives, latency and 4XX/5XX error rates, not on CPU, because a customer never complained about CPU. Breaches go to Slack, where the on-call engineer is, rather than to an email nobody reads.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Monitoring does not stop at the infrastructure layer, and most of what breaks in a data platform is not the infrastructure. The table lists what is watched where, and what happens when it trips. Everything in it is code and everything in it has a defined action; a signal without an action is a screensaver.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The last two rows matter as much as the first. A tracing schema for the LLM assistant that stores fourteen fields, a salted user hash and a team, and never a name or a tool output, is an observability decision and a privacy decision at once, and it is the reason the traces can be kept. The surf verifier on this site found a wave model returning nulls beyond lead three on its first day of collection, and reported it as a finding rather than dropping the rows. That is what monitoring is for.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Access is least privilege by construction, in Terraform: per-project groups with read-only access everywhere and write access only in a personal sandbox, replacing the blanket "full analyst" role a new joiner used to get on day one. Partner databases moved from static credentials to RDS IAM authentication through assume-role chains with short-lived tokens, so there is no password to rotate and nothing to paste into a chat. Between the clouds, Workload Identity Federation does the same job at the platform level.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The same discipline applies to AI agents, where it is newer and rarer. An autonomous agent is scoped so it cannot reach resources outside its remit. A service-account-backed assistant turned out to be a confused deputy, a user could make the assistant's credentials do what the user's own could not, and the fix was per-domain protection domains enforced at BigQuery IAM, not a line in the prompt. The assistant's MCP surface, forty exposed tools of which eighteen could write, was cut to a fifteen-tool read-only allowlist, with a project-scoping wrapper that rejects out-of-scope queries before they reach the warehouse. A prompt is a suggestion. IAM is a wall.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The habit predates the job. I studied data science and cybersecurity at VŠE (thesis in pattern engineering for cybersecurity, nominated for the national IT SPY award in 2025), spent a year in fraud and forensic analytics at EY, and when an independent security review of FilmRunner came back I acted on all of it: an IS_DEV blocklist that failed open on a blank environment variable became an explicit allowlist, and SSO auto-provisioning was gated on a server-side SAML claim rather than a client assertion.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: dbt modernisation: Python models on Dataproc/Spark for latency-sensitive transformations such as NLP and language detection, a BigQuery materialisation and cost strategy, incremental models with unique keys over self-referential deltas. Dagster orchestrates extracts containerised as Docker images across many portal sources; multi-organisation CRM extraction was made resilient so that one organisation's missing entity skips instead of aborting the run for everyone else.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The choice between SQL and Python models is a cost choice, not a taste choice. A language-detection pass over job adverts is a Python model on Spark because BigQuery would do it slowly and expensively; a daily salary aggregate is SQL because the warehouse does aggregates better than anything I could write. Materialisation follows the same logic: incremental where the delta is identifiable by a key, table where it is not, view where nobody reads it often enough to pay for storage.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The cutover I am proudest of is boring on purpose. A legacy salary-recompute pipeline moved from a standalone extractor to an incremental dbt-python model. Before a single downstream consumer was repointed, the new model was proven byte-identical to the old one across five years of history: zero mismatches across twenty columns. Shipped with backups, freshness tests and a git-revert rollback path. Same habit on a production GA4 event-stream backfill: validated by full-row fingerprint, 62 of 62 days identical to the pre-backfill snapshot, dev ≡ prod, and the one-off operation kept out of the production codebase.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The method is simple and I use it everywhere: compute both sides, key them, diff every column with a tolerance for floats, hash each day's rows and compare the hashes, and only then touch the consumers. On this site the hockey atlas's graph ingest is preceded by the same idea in miniature: a read-only merge check computes the ids it would write and counts collisions before it mutates anything, which caught a bug that would have created about 570 phantom players. The number that matters in a migration is the one that says nothing changed.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The long version of this section, with the architecture, the protocol and the lessons, is AI over data, measured.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The goal: non-technical staff self-serve BI questions and analysts stop being the bottleneck. The build: a LangGraph agent behind FastAPI on the Anthropic API, with MCP connectors to BigQuery, OpenMetadata and Metabase. The first decision was to replace a ~4 500-line bespoke NL→SQL service (Vanna, ChromaDB, a custom pipeline) with a ~400-line agent whose domain knowledge lives in the data catalogue instead of the codebase, chosen on maintenance cost per line, at parity on the golden question sets.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Then the trust layer, which is what Quaesitor is about: every figure the assistant returns is cross-checked against certified BI dashboards, lookup is catalogue-first, and protocol compliance is an explicit evaluation metric, not a hope. Then hardening after measuring: the tool allowlist and scoping wrapper above, and hard caps, added after a single unbounded question consumed 4.07 million input tokens and $21 without failing. The eval harness over verified golden sets found a malformed output schema in a third-party MCP server that was silently discarding results, non-deterministically; without the harness that would have been "the assistant is sometimes wrong". The first business POC ran with the stakeholders in the room: their real questions became date-fixed golden cases, ambiguous definitions (category semantics, tier models, credit balances) were driven to authoritative answers and written into the OpenMetadata glossary, so the agent inherits them instead of re-deriving them per question.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: A multi-app repository migrated from Poetry to uv, lockfile resolution from about thirty seconds to under one per app. Dependabot alerts cut from 792 to 332 through dependency and Python-pin cleanup across fifteen library manifests and eight apps. The internal documentation site rebuilt on Zensical with the Diátaxis structure, tutorials apart from reference apart from explanation, so an analyst can get a first app running without reading CDK internals. Onboarding is an access-design problem as much as a documentation problem; the Terraform groups in section 4 are what makes day one safe, and the docs are what makes it short.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Infrastructure as code, always. Least privilege as the default, for people and for agents. Read-only verification before mutating shared state. Parity and fingerprint validation before any cutover. Decisions written down as ADRs with the rejected options kept. Evaluation harnesses and golden sets before anyone calls a model "good". Cost guardrails sized from measured runs, not from hope. An honest limitations section in every report, including the ones on this site. Documentation in the Diátaxis shape. And no figure typed by hand anywhere a script could have produced it.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: Golemio, Prague's city data platform (2024–2025): senior member of the three-person transport data team, Scrum lead, mentoring on ML practice. Architected the ML platform, Kafka to dbt/Prefect to Docker/Kubernetes to a prediction API, and ran the production pipeline serving bus-arrival predictions for the city's fleet to the city's apps, on PostgreSQL/PostGIS and Azure, at terabytes a month. The vehicle-location records behind the record and the thesis come from there; so does the finding that the delays are not predictable in the way the pipeline hoped, which is on this site too. I spoke about the work at the Prague City Data Congress in 2025 and at Smart City Expo in Barcelona in 2024. Medicalc (2024): statistical models for real-time patient monitoring in C++ with a zero-defect requirement. ČSFD, the Czech film database (2022–2024): backend and data engineering for one of the largest Czech sites: the movie database and its query performance, a collaborative-filtering recommender, an ETL pipeline over twenty external sources (VOD platforms, cinemas) and the migration from a monolith to microservices. EY, forensics and fraud (2021–2022): pattern recognition, anomaly detection and fuzzy entity resolution across financial datasets, presented to executives and regulators, which is where the habit of defending every figure line by line comes from.

passages.title: The platform is code. So is the trust.
passages.text: The same habits, in public, where they can be checked. The model release watch runs the Quaesitor harness (524 tests) monthly from a launchd job with the operator's own tool configuration stripped, indexes every report with its fingerprints and cost, and pushes a data file the page renders from. The surf forecast verification is a GitHub Actions cron with append-only JSON, idempotent collectors, data-quality counts that found a model dropout on day one, sample-size gates, block-bootstrap intervals and a six-test suite that has to pass before a number is shown. The hockey atlas's graph ingest has the read-only merge check from section 6. The football atlas was built spec → plan → task agents → reviews, with 163 tests and 23 dated rulings. And Quaesitor's site refused to build when a run stopped supporting a sentence. That rule is on every page here. Whether each of these jobs actually ran, how fresh its data is against the cadence it promised and what it cost is on the status page, read live from the same files and from GitHub; what the site itself changed, commit by commit, is on the changelog, generated from git log at every deploy. The domain itself is code too: the Cloudflare zone (DNS, the www-to-apex redirect, security headers on every response, HTTPS only, TLS 1.2 or better) is Terraform in infra/, adopted by declarative imports so nothing was recreated, and the Worker that serves the site deploys from the repository on every push.

passages.title: The living call sheet
passages.text: Film call sheets follow conventions that are decades old and load-bearing. Same-day revisions are the norm, named by colour or letter, so the sheet has to be a container of ordered revisions, not one mutable row, or "what changed since the version I printed" cannot be answered. Page counts are in eighths of a page, because scripts are timed that way, so they are stored as an integer eighth-count rather than a float an assistant director does arithmetic on by hand. Cast status codes (W, SW, WF, H, SWF, R) are a constrained enum. And offline is not a nice-to-have: call times are 5–6 am, locations are outside coverage, and this is the one document all 50 to 200 people need before they leave home.

passages.title: The living call sheet
passages.text: End-to-end production management for mid-budget films: script import, an AI-drafted breakdown, a stripboard schedule with a cascade engine, and the published call sheet in every crew member's pocket. Around it, the track a studio's procurement asks for: SSO/SAML with organisation domain mapping and post-login auto-provisioning, legal pages and a DPA, an in-app help hub, Sentry with a PII-scrubbing hook, opt-in PostHog analytics, and Stripe, Twilio, Resend, Frame.io and Google Calendar integrations. Real-time over WebSockets with unified subprotocol auth; an offline-first PWA for on-set conditions.

passages.title: The living call sheet
passages.text: An independent security review found two things worth keeping as lessons: an IS_DEV blocklist that failed open on a blank environment variable, inverted into an explicit allowlist; and SSO auto-provisioning gated on a client assertion, moved to a server-side SAML claim.

passages.title: The living call sheet
passages.text: The skeleton keeps only the call-sheet slice: creating, revising and distributing shoot-day sheets, viewable offline. No budgeting, no breakdowns, no scheduling optimiser, no billing; what was deferred and why is written down before the code. FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2.0, Alembic and PostgreSQL behind; a React + Vite + TypeScript PWA in front, IndexedDB cache and a Workbox service worker, so a published day still renders in airplane mode. Sign-in by e-mail code, no password; owners invite editors and viewers and the API enforces the role. The API runs on Fly.io in Frankfurt with Supabase as plain Postgres; five architecture decision records cover the frontend stack, hosting, the editor, auth and roles.

passages.title: The living call sheet
passages.text: The company itself runs as one founder and an AI team, with an operating model, an approval contract and a rule that nothing with real-world effect happens without an approved item in an inbox file. That is written down too, in the repository, because a process that lives only in someone's head is not a process.

passages.title: The living call sheet
passages.text: The live demo serves the PWA from GitHub Pages with a bundled sample shoot day. Open it on a phone, add it to the home screen, switch to airplane mode: the call sheet still renders from the cache. The AD editor is the other side of it.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: The same question as the hockey atlas, asked of football with a better corpus: how deep is the Czech pool per head, where does the pathway abroad leak, what is the World Cup squad made of, and what do Norway and Denmark do that Czechia does not. Czechia is the worked example. The pipeline takes a nationality code and a peer set.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: 35 % Switzerland 88 % · Norway 65 %

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: The atlas maps every Czech professional FBref knows about, 440 players, 192 of them with a full 2025/26 season in one of nineteen leagues, and reads the pool the way a federation would want to: against peers, per head, along the pathway abroad, and at the moment a tournament squad is named. No predictions, no selection advice. Every number on the page is computed from the run and the build refuses to render a sentence its data no longer supports; there are 163 tests and a ledger of 23 rulings behind it.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: Count the distinct players with at least 450 minutes on a 2025/26 roster in the nine strongest European leagues, divide by population. Czechia has 26, which is 2.39 per million.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: Seventh of nine. Denmark, with half the population, has five times the density; Slovakia, again, is ahead. The largest cohort gap is midfielders aged 23 to 25: two Czech players in the top-9 leagues against a peer median of six. Defenders under 22: none, against a peer median of 1.5.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: Three numbers along the road from a Czech academy to a top-9 roster. Minutes at home: players aged 21 or younger get 6.4 % of all minutes in the Czech First League; in Denmark 15.3 %, Hungary 14.1 %, Croatia 14.0 %, Norway 11.5 %. Where they go: 27 of the 192 mapped players play abroad; 63 % of them in a top-9 league, but 19 % moved sideways, to a league no stronger than the Czech one by the multiplier. How they fare: Czech exports keep a median 50 % of their club's minutes, third of nine countries of origin, behind Slovakia (76 %) and Hungary (57 %) and ahead of Denmark (46 %) and Norway (37 %). Fewer leave; the ones who do, play.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: And the squad. Of the 26 players named for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, 35 % play in the nine strongest leagues. Switzerland's squad: 88 %. Croatia 73 %, Austria 69 %, Norway 65 %.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: Count Czech players with at least 450 minutes in the Big-5 leagues, every season since 2000/01. The peak is 26 in 2007/08 (the most-minutes names that season: Drobný, Plašil, Kučera; in 2002/03 Čech, Koller, Jarolím). The trough is 6 in 2015/16. The current figure is 10. Denmark is at 38 and Croatia at 24, both on a rising line.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: fig. 1 · Czech players in the Big-5 leagues, 2000/01 to 2025/26, against eight peers (grey). Lower panel: the same per million. Recoloured to this site's palette from the atlas render.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: This is presence, not quality: goalkeepers count, a lineup of who was there. But it dates the problem. The decline is not recent and it is not a blip; it is a fifteen-year line with a floor in it.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: The same six numbers, same definitions, same seasons. A comparison, not a causal claim.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: The export age is the same everywhere, 22. What differs is what happens before it (minutes at home) and what the export leads to (a top-9 roster, or a sideways move). Norway gives its under-21s twice the domestic minutes and sends 65 % of its squad to the top nine; Denmark gives them two and a half times the minutes and loses a tenth of its exports sideways against Czechia's fifth.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: Every player-season is one five-feature vector, identical across all nineteen leagues because only the basic table exists for all of them: non-penalty goals and assists per 90, share of club minutes, age, cards per 90. Rates for players with few minutes are shrunk towards the median of their league and season with \(K = 10\) phantom matches, \(\hat r = (\text{events} + K\cdot 90\,\tilde r)/(\text{minutes} + K\cdot 90)\); at the 450-minute floor the league median carries 67 % of the weight, at 900 minutes the player and the median weigh the same. PCA to two components, K-means, drawn twice: a style map on raw rates and a quality map with the league multiplier applied first.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: fig. 2 · Midfielders 2025/26, style and quality projections. The cohort with the largest gap. Rings mark a national-team call-up 2024–26.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: The multipliers are UEFA association coefficients, current five-year ranking, normalised to the strongest league (Premier League 1.000, Serie A 0.856, Bundesliga 0.788, Czech First League 0.434, Slovak Super Liga 0.217); second tiers at 0.6 of their country's first tier, a stated assumption. ClubElo was the plan and was unreachable at run time, which the atlas says rather than hides. So each multiplier was perturbed ±20 % on its own and all of them together, 41 scenarios; 37 change nobody in the union of the three position groups' top tens, and the largest churn is one player, on the Czech league's own multiplier.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: The data-quality log is on the page, with counts: 92 women's entries dropped from FBref's country page by surname (the rule and its limits are stated), 2 namesakes disambiguated by club, 125 professionals in leagues without season tables listed by name only, 441 split-season rows collapsed after mid-season transfers, 18 call-up names that match no row. Every wrangling decision that changed a count, with the count.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: The UEFA multipliers are one estimate of what a league is worth. The atlas carries a second, and the two do not have to agree. League strength from the transfer graph: a hierarchical Poisson model of non-penalty goals plus assists per 90, fitted in PyMC on the 2 125 players observed in at least two leagues across 8 108 qualifying player-seasons and seven seasons. Only a mover's own before-and-after separates his level from the league's scoring environment; a model on all players recovers the environment instead (open, high-scoring Eredivisie reads as the strongest league, tight Serie A as the weakest), which is why the corpus is restricted to movers, the same within-subject logic as plus-minus ratings in other team sports. Sampled with NUTS, no divergences, R-hat ≤ 1.003.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: In these terms a Czech First League season is worth 0.67 of a Premier League one (90 % HDI 0.59–0.75), against 0.434 from the UEFA coefficient. The two rankings correlate at Spearman 0.74 over eighteen leagues and disagree loudly in places: Hungary's NB I is sixth by the movers and seventeenth by UEFA; the Eredivisie fifteenth and eighth. Held out on the 2025–26 season (863 candidates), the model predicts next-season production better than either the UEFA multiplier or a naive carry-forward, log predictive density −2.17 against −2.73 and −2.63, mean absolute error 0.127 against 0.151 and 0.137. The map on this page still uses the UEFA numbers, because the sensitivity table above was run on them; the atlas shows both and says which is which.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: Two more models sit beside it. Three models, one task, five seasons: predict a player's league-adjusted production next season from this one, evaluated by rolling-origin cross-validation over five target seasons and 8 850 test pairs. A gradient-boosted regressor wins on pooled RMSE, 0.0706, with the hierarchical Bayesian regression at 0.0713 and persistence at 0.0754; the Bayesian model is the only one that reports an interval, and its 90 % interval covers 91.6 % of outcomes. The multilayer perceptron does not beat the boosting. Dating the break: the count of Czech players in the top-9 leagues, 26 → 6 → 10 since 2007, modelled as a local level with one step change at an unknown season; the change-point falls in 2014–15 with 62 % posterior probability, a ×0.57 (0.38–0.86) drop in the level. A rolling-origin backtest over fifteen origins scores the same model without the step against "same as last season": MAE 2.8 against 2.7, 90 % coverage 0.87, which is to say the forecast is honest and no better than the naive one, and the one forecast made, 11 (5–18) for 2026–27, is a demonstration of the method on a count, not a statement about any player.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: And the question of the previous section, put as a regression: across the eight peer countries, a Bayesian simple regression of top-9 players per million on the U21 share of domestic minutes gives +10.1 per ten percentage points (90 % HDI −1.7 to +23.3, R² 0.27, n = 8), the same sign as a pooled-panel OLS at +7.8 (1.1–14.0); the interval is wide because the panel is small, and the page says so. A ridge decomposition of the gap into three channels, in the linear form of Blinder–Oaxaca, attributes Norway's +7.0 players per million over Czechia mostly to U21 minutes (+4.2) and league strength (+5.1), and Denmark's +10.2 mostly to U21 minutes (+7.4).

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: A written design spec, an implementation plan of small tasks, a fresh coding agent per task, a spec-compliance and code-quality review after each, a whole-branch review at the end, and every decision the controller took without me written down as a dated ruling: 23 of them for the first edition. I wrote the framing, the cluster reads and the rulings; the agents wrote the code under the tests. The whole thing is one repository: pipeline, models, validation, report, site. From a clean clone, uv sync && make restore-snapshot && make render reproduces the report from the committed snapshot without touching the network.

passages.title: When did the train leave, and where does it stop
passages.text: The live atlas, with 17 player cards chosen by six stated rules, interactive projections and the Czech edition, is at football.bsandova.com. The Bayesian layer described in the next section is on the same page, chapter IV of the methodology.

passages.text: Hockey intuition knows the Czech pool player by player. It has no single place where the structure is added up against Finland, Sweden and Slovakia. So I built one: 385 players, two projections, one number that nobody had aggregated, and two analyses that did not survive their own review.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: The atlas is a map of the Czech professional player pool, read through data rather than reputation: every active player with Czech eligibility in the NHL, Liiga and the Tipsport Extraliga, segmented by position and playing profile, with the national-team cycle laid over it. It makes no predictions and recommends no roster. It is a methodological tool for watching a pool over a four-year cycle, and it exists because the structural comparison with peer countries is the kind of thing everyone in hockey knows in fragments and nobody holds in one place.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: Take every player with birth_country = CZE on a 2025/26 NHL roster, fifteen of them, and divide by 10.9 million inhabitants. Do the same for five peer countries. Czechia lands fifth of six.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: The USA has the most NHL players in absolute terms and a population of 340 million to dilute them. Slovakia, with half the Czech population, outranks Czechia. Finland's density is roughly four times higher, Sweden's five. None of this is news to a scout; the point is that the number now has a definition and a source, and can be recomputed next season by anyone.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: Split the NHL contingent by position and age and the structure shows. Each cell is the number of players and their median points per game.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: The Czech U22 forward cohort in the NHL is one player: Kulich. Finland has three, Sweden seven. The 26–29 elite, Pastrňák, Nečas, Zacha, Hertl, holds a median of 1.06 points per game, world class by any reading, and is four players deep. Defence is the structural problem at every age: four Czech defencemen in the NHL in total, against Finland's fourteen and Sweden's thirty, and none under 22.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: Every player is a four-dimensional vector (goals, assists and penalty minutes per game, age), projected with PCA and clustered with K-means, the number of clusters chosen by silhouette. The atlas draws it twice. The style map uses raw per-game rates and shows the playing profile: Pastrňák and Červenka sit in the same production zone, because in their own leagues they produce alike. The quality map multiplies each rate by a league factor first, and the NHL elite pulls away, Pastrňák at PC1 ≈ 8.5 against Červenka at ≈ 2. Showing both, side by side, means the effect of the league adjustment is visible instead of baked in, and the reader does not have to accept a single narrative.

passages.text: fig. 1 · Forwards 2025/26 in both projections. Rings mark the World Championship 24/25 pool; arrows point from 2024/25 to 2025/26. Recoloured to this site's palette from the atlas render; the geometry is unchanged.

passages.text: fig. 2 · Defencemen, same interpretation. Six clusters, from offensive puck-movers (Hronek) to defensive depth.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: The forwards fall into four archetypes: top-six scorers (18 players, median birth year 1996), young prospects and depth (122, mostly Extraliga, median 2001), physical role players (9, penalty minutes five to six times the cohort median) and veteran two-way forwards (92). The national-team pool, 42 of the 81 players who played the 2024 or 2025 World Championship, spans all of them and both ecosystems: it is neither an NHL contingent nor an Extraliga contingent, it is the bridge.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: Per-game rates lie when the sample is tiny. A player with four games and five points, 1.25 P/GP raw, would outrank Pastrňák. So rates are shrunk towards their league median with an empirical-Bayes prior, \(K = 10\) phantom games:

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: At one game the median dominates (about 91 %); at eighty the player's own data does (about 89 %). The four-game player drops to 0.59 P/GP, which is where a four-game sample belongs.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: The league multipliers are the honest weak point: NHL 1.00, AHL 0.55, SHL 0.45, Liiga 0.42, NL 0.40, Extraliga 0.35, first league 0.20, approximations informed by public NHL-equivalency work. So they were perturbed by ±20 % each and the quality ranking recomputed: the top ten changes by at most one player in any scenario, the mean rank shift in the top twenty stays under five places, and the NHL top four stay the top four everywhere. The map is not sensitive to the thing I was least sure of.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: An age-production curve for the Extraliga came out looking like players improve into their thirties. They do not; the ones still playing at 33 are the ones good enough to still be playing, and the curve was survivorship. An early attempt at youth-to-Extraliga conversion was right-censored, because the historical youth rosters had not been scraped yet and the recent ones had not had time to convert. Both were dropped before publishing and the atlas says so. A method that cannot say what its data cannot show is not a method.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita

The patterns are hypotheses for someone with the internal data to validate, not conclusions.

passages.title: Who Czech hockey produces, per capita
passages.text: Above the structural layer sits an applied one: a Neo4j knowledge graph of about 3 200 players across NHL, AHL, Extraliga, Liiga, SHL and the Swiss NL, with identity resolution on name, date of birth and position across sources; FAISS similarity search in the style space; historical career analogs from a corpus of 1 177 players; and per-player scouting briefs drafted by an LLM under grounding rules (names reproduced verbatim, position-filtered similarity, regular-season stats labelled as such). Every ingest that mutates the graph is preceded by a read-only merge check that computes the ids it would write and counts collisions first; that check caught a duplicate-node bug that would have created about 570 phantom players.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: The assignment recreates a COVID-19 study in which physiological measurements from emergency care predict a patient's outcome. Mine was the P/F ratio, PaO2/FiO2 in kPa, the standard measure of oxygenation and the number used to grade acute respiratory distress. 622 patients, fourteen readings each, one label, exactly balanced: 311 Improving, 311 Deteriorating. No identifiers, so the only thing linking a row of readings to its label is position, and the first assertion in the notebook is that the two files line up. No missing values at all, which in clinical records is implausible, and the reason turned up later.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: A higher P/F ratio means better oxygenation; a falling one is what deterioration in respiratory distress looks like. In this dataset the group labelled Deteriorating has the higher ratio, 23.8 against 18.9 kPa, and the rising trend, +0.11 against −0.29 kPa per half-day. Level and direction both point the wrong way.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: That could be a peculiarity of one variable, so I ran the other nine feature files against the same label file. Against identical labels the Deteriorating group has lower CRP, lower lactate, lower peak pressure, lower PaCO2, higher oxygen saturation, higher pH, higher bicarbonate and higher platelets: nine of ten level differences significant at p < 0.001, all describing the "deteriorating" patients as the healthier and recovering ones. The tenth, ventilatory ratio, differs on nothing and sits around 1 300 for a quantity that should be near 1–3, so that file is mis-scaled. The nine are not one measurement counted nine times: their per-patient means correlate at 0.21 on average, and the eigenvalues of that matrix imply about eight independent tests. What they share is the cohort, so this is one finding observed nine ways, not nine replications.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: fig. 1 · Mean P/F ratio with 95 % confidence bands, cleaned dataset (n = 621). The group called Deteriorating is the one getting better. Recomputed from the CSVs for this page; matches the report.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: The competing explanation is that the label file is shifted against the readings. A random shuffle is out, because it would destroy the signal rather than reverse it. A structured shift is not, so I tested the row order itself. It is strongly non-random: a Wald–Wolfowitz runs test on the label column gives 241 runs against an expected 312 ± 12.5, z = −5.66. But the structure is not spread through the file. The first 500 rows are in perfectly random order (z = −0.44); what the global test sees is one changepoint near row 500, after which the Deteriorating share drops from 59.6 % to 10.7 %.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: fig. 2 · Share of rows labelled Deteriorating by position in the label file, bins of 100. A single changepoint near row 500; χ²(6) = 101.5.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: Then the direct test. If the files were offset, realigning them should strengthen the association. Scanning offsets from −30 to +30 and testing the group difference at each, the association is strongest at exactly zero (t = +8.84), the nearest competitor is less than half as strong, and no offset in the range produces a significant association in the clinically expected direction. Realigning never restores the expected sign. Misalignment is ruled out; mislabelling stands, and the odd row order is a second, separate defect that affects nothing downstream because the split is stratified and shuffled. Every clinical sentence in the report carries the caveat that the class called Deteriorating behaves like a recovering patient.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: One record fails integrity: patient 84 holds 22.166667 at all fourteen timepoints. Fourteen measurements over seven days do not agree to six decimals, and 22.166667 is 66.5/3, which is what a single value carried forward looks like. Removed; it is also the proof that imputation happened upstream. Then Tukey's rule, column by column, flags 128 patients, a fifth of the cohort. The variable is right-skewed at every timepoint (mean absolute skew 1.75), Tukey assumes symmetry, and on skewed data the upper fence just cuts through a smoothly decaying tail. On the log scale skew drops to 0.24.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: Accuracy spans 0.018 across the five, against a fold-to-fold standard deviation of about 0.04, so it cannot decide anything. What decides it is who gets deleted: the naive rule removes 85 Deteriorating patients against 43 Improving, because that is the higher-valued class and Tukey only has an upper fence to trip. It would turn a balanced dataset into 268/225 while deleting exactly the readings that carry the signal. So the primary dataset winsorises at the log-scale fences instead: 97 readings out of 8 694, 1.12 %, capped across 57 patients, nobody deleted, balance intact. The leakage from fitting fences on the whole set was measured rather than worried about: refitting them inside each fold moves SVC accuracy from 0.7681 to 0.7679.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: Neither group has a dramatic course: Improving drifts from 20.0 to 16.9 kPa, Deteriorating from 22.4 to 24.6. What grows is the gap between them. All fourteen timepoints separate the groups after Benjamini–Hochberg correction, which at n = 621 is nearly unavoidable, so the effect size is the informative number: Cohen's d rises almost monotonically from 0.22 on the first morning, below the threshold for a small effect, to 0.95 on the seventh evening, a large one. A single admission reading carries almost nothing; a week of them carries a great deal.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: fig. 3 · Cohen's d between the groups at each timepoint, equal-n pooled SD. Mint: medium effect and above; acid: large. Recomputed from the CSVs; identical to the report's table.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: Adjacent timepoints correlate at r = 0.71, decaying to 0.38 across the week: the fourteen columns are one smooth trajectory, not fourteen measurements. That predicts two things, both tested. Regularisation matters for logistic regression (at C = 10 the coefficients of adjacent timepoints oscillate between −0.33 and +0.20; at C = 0.01 they settle into a profile rising towards day seven). And hand-built summary features should add nothing: adding mean, SD, slope, change and the two day averages moves nested accuracy by +0.014, −0.007 and +0.001. No gain.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: Logistic regression, an RBF support vector classifier and a random forest, one shared stratified 80/20 split, scaling inside the pipeline, grids of 7, 20 and 20 candidates. On the held-out 125 patients the forest scores 0.792, the SVC 0.776, logistic regression 0.736, against a 0.504 baseline. That is the obvious reading and it does not survive.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: The three models are scored on the same test set, so their accuracies are paired and McNemar's exact test is the comparison: p = 0.44, 0.14 and 0.83 for the three pairs. The resampled comparison had the same flaw in a subtler form: re-scoring an already-tuned model lets every test fold contain patients that chose its hyperparameters. Nesting the whole grid search inside every outer fold costs the SVC 0.028, the forest 0.009, logistic regression 0.006, and reorders the top two. With the Nadeau–Bengio correction for shared training data, p = 0.26, 0.22 and 0.60. Nothing separates them. All three extract about the same signal, 0.70 to 0.74 against 0.50.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: The SVC's grid spans 0.623 to 0.762, a range of 0.139, which is wider than the gap between the best and worst model: choosing γ badly costs more than choosing the wrong algorithm. Its selected setting sits on an isolated peak of the grid, which is what a search that fits the folds rather than the problem looks like, and is why its selection optimism is the largest. The forest's four most important timepoints are the four with the largest effect sizes, D7 PM, D7 AM, D6 PM, D6 AM, though across all fourteen the rank correlation is ρ = 0.49, p = 0.078: corroboration, not replication.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: So which would I deploy? Logistic regression. Repeating everything on the row-deleted dataset moves it by 0.001 where the SVC moves 0.033 and the forest 0.049; its regularised coefficients can be shown to a clinician; its reported number carries the least optimism. Unless the model is used for triage with a tuned threshold, in which case what matters is ranking, and the forest's AUC of 0.852 against 0.809 makes it the better choice. The case is stated with the circumstance that would flip it.

passages.title: The label says deteriorating. The patient is getting better.
passages.text: Check the direction of the labels before anything else, and check it with every variable you have, not just the one you were assigned. Test the row order. When a cleaning rule deletes a fifth of the cohort, look at who it deletes, because "accuracy did not change" is not the same as "nothing changed". Tune inside the loop or the number is not the number. And when three models are indistinguishable, say so; the useful answer is often the one the leaderboard reading gets wrong.

passages.text: Text 01 said Prague lost about 2 745 stalls to longer cars, and borrowed the growth of the cars from a European series. Its own limitations section named the next step: measure it on cars registered in Czechia. This is that step. The growth to 2022 survives to the millimetre. The number does not, because the last three years were an assumption, and an assumption is where the two sources part.
